title: Datagram Transport Layer Security Version 1.2
summary: Specifies version 1.2 of Datagram Transport Layer Security, which gives communications privacy for datagram protocols. It is based on TLS and designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery, while allowing for datagram behavior such as loss and reordering. It was replaced by RFC 9147.

eli5.summary: TLS keeps web chats secret, but it needs messages to arrive in order. DTLS does the same for messages that may get lost or shuffled, like secret postcards. Replaced by RFC 9147.

questions: how does dtls differ from tls
what is the dtls cookie exchange
subtitle: TLS 1.2 adapted to survive lost, reordered and duplicated datagrams, such as those carried over UDP.

tldr.problem: TLS needs a reliable, in-order transport such as TCP, so it breaks when packets are lost or reordered. Applications built on UDP were left with unsatisfactory security choices.
tldr.mechanism: DTLS makes the smallest changes to TLS 1.2 that fix this: explicit record sequence numbers and epochs, a stateless cookie exchange, handshake fragmentation and retransmission timers.
tldr.outcome: DTLS 1.2 became the datagram counterpart to TLS 1.2. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 9147, which defines DTLS 1.3.

facts.label: Initial retransmit timer
facts.value: 1 second, doubling up to at least 60 seconds

today: RFC 6347 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 9147. It was also updated by RFC 7507, RFC 7905, RFC 8996, RFC 9146 and RFC 10015, so new work should follow the newer specification.

sections.title: Why TLS Needs a Datagram Version
sections.content:
TLS gives applications a transparent, connection-oriented secure channel, but it must run over a reliable transport, typically TCP. That rules it out for traffic carried over unreliable datagrams. The RFC points to protocols such as the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and electronic gaming, which increasingly use UDP.

Designers of those applications had unsatisfactory options: use IPsec, which suits only some applications, or design a custom application-layer security protocol, which takes a large amount of effort. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) is the third option. It is deliberately as similar to TLS as possible, to minimize new security invention and maximize code reuse.

DTLS 1.2 is defined as a series of deltas to TLS 1.2. There is no DTLS 1.1; that number was skipped to harmonize version numbers with TLS. The protocol runs in application space and does not compensate for lost or reordered payload data, so media streaming, telephony and gaming behave the same as before.
sections.eli5: Normal secret messaging needs every letter to arrive in order. Some programs, like games and phone calls, would rather skip a lost letter than wait, so they needed a secret code that works with missing letters.

sections.title: How DTLS Fixes TLS for Unreliable Transport
sections.content:
Unreliability breaks TLS at two levels. First, TLS records cannot be decrypted independently: the integrity check depends on an implicit sequence number, so a lost record N makes the check on record N+1 fail. Second, the TLS handshake assumes its messages are delivered reliably and in order.

DTLS handles the first problem by banning stream ciphers and carrying an explicit sequence number in every record. It handles the second with a retransmission timer, a sequence number on each handshake message so out-of-order messages can be queued, and fragmentation so large handshake messages fit in a datagram. TLS handshake messages can in theory be up to 2^24-1 bytes, while UDP datagrams are often kept under 1500 bytes.

DTLS also optionally supports replay detection with a bitmap window of received records, the same technique used in IPsec AH/ESP. It is optional because duplication is not always malicious and can be caused by routing errors.
sections.eli5: Every card gets a number so it can be read even if the one before it is missing. Big messages are torn into small pieces that each fit in one envelope, and if no reply comes, the sender tries again.

sections.title: The DTLS Record Layer
sections.content:
The record layer is nearly the same as in TLS 1.2. The change is two new fields: a 16-bit epoch and a 48-bit sequence_number. The epoch starts at zero and increments each time a ChangeCipherSpec message is sent, which lets the receiver tell apart records from different cipher states that carry the same sequence number. Sequence numbers are kept separately for each epoch.

DTLS 1.2 uses the on-the-wire version { 254, 253 }, the 1's complement of the version number, which keeps its records easy to tell apart from TLS. The MAC uses the 64-bit value formed by joining the epoch and sequence number.

Each record MUST fit in a single datagram, though several records may share one datagram and none may span datagrams. Records carry no association identifier, so applications must multiplex associations themselves, for example by host and port with UDP. The RFC also bans RC4: it cannot be randomly accessed, so it MUST NOT be used with DTLS.

Receivers SHOULD silently discard invalid records instead of ending the connection. If an implementation does send an alert, it MUST be fatal, and doing so over UDP is NOT RECOMMENDED because forged datagrams are so easy to produce.
sections.eli5: Each card now has a round number and a card number written on it. If a card is damaged or a copy shows up twice, the reader quietly throws it away rather than hanging up the whole call.

sections.title: The Handshake: Cookies, Fragments and Retransmission
sections.content:
DTLS uses the same handshake messages and flows as TLS 1.2 with three principal changes: a stateless cookie exchange, a changed handshake header, and retransmission timers.

The cookie exchange counters two denial-of-service attacks: exhausting server resources with handshake requests, and using the server as an amplifier by forging the victim's address. The server MAY answer a ClientHello with a HelloVerifyRequest holding a cookie, and the client MUST resend its ClientHello with the cookie added. A suggested cookie is HMAC(Secret, Client-IP, Client-Parameters), so the server keeps no per-client state. Servers SHOULD do the exchange for every new handshake, and clients MUST be ready for it. It gives no defense against attacks from valid addresses.

The handshake header gains message_seq, fragment_offset and fragment_length. A message split into fragments keeps the same message_seq, and receivers buffer fragments until the whole message is present.

Messages are grouped into flights that are retransmitted as a unit. Implementations SHOULD start with a 1 second timer and double it at each retransmission, up to no less than 60 seconds. The node that sends the last flight MUST keep answering a retransmit of the peer's last flight for at least twice the default MSL defined for TCP, to avoid deadlock if that flight was lost.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the server sends the visitor a secret code word and only goes on if the visitor says it back. That stops pranksters who lie about their address. Messages are sent in batches, and if no answer comes in a second, the batch is sent again, waiting longer each time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because DTLS is a variant of TLS 1.2, most security considerations are those of TLS 1.2, in its appendices D, E and F. The main additional concern is denial of service.

The cookie exchange is the defense. Servers that skip it can be used as attack amplifiers even when they are not themselves under attack, so they SHOULD use it unless amplification is not a threat in their environment. A server can defend against collected, reused cookies by changing its secret frequently, optionally accepting two secrets for a short window.

The RFC also asks that a DTLS server that sees an epoch 0 ClientHello on an existing association not destroy that association until the client proves it is reachable, by completing a cookie exchange or a handshake with a verifiable Finished message. That stops off-path attackers from tearing down associations with forged ClientHellos.
sections.eli5: The big danger is someone using the server to throw rocks at a stranger by lying about who is asking. The code-word check makes sure whoever asks can really receive the answer.

sections.title: IANA Considerations and Changes from DTLS 1.0
sections.content:
DTLS shares the TLS identifier space, so no new registries are needed. IANA added a DTLS-OK flag to the TLS parameter registries, and authors of new identifiers MUST say whether they suit DTLS. All TLS 1.2 registrations are suitable except the RC4 cipher suites and a few exporter labels that the RFC lists. The new hello_verify_request handshake type was assigned the value 3.

Compared with DTLS 1.0, this version updates the protocol to match TLS 1.2, adds AEAD cipher support, clarifies sequence numbers and epochs, adds a procedure for state loss, tightens path MTU rules, prohibits epoch wrapping, and recommends a fixed version number in the HelloVerifyRequest.
sections.eli5: The rule book says which TLS ingredients are safe for the postcard version and which are not, and notes what changed since the first edition.
